cases.interviewerQuestion: When you and your co-lead were both learning Spanner and Dataflow from scratch, what was the first major assumption from your SQL background that turned out to be wrong once you started designing the schema and migration pipeline?
cases.tonyRaw: The big one was assuming primary key design could carry over mostly unchanged. In traditional SQL you often key off monotonically increasing IDs and let the database handle it, but Spanner splits data across nodes by key range, so sequential keys create hotspots where all your write traffic slams into one split instead of distributing evenly. We had to rethink key structure for distribution — things like hashing or using more randomized/composite keys — which fed directly into how we designed the migration pipeline in Dataflow, since we couldn't just lift-and-shift the schema. That realization early on saved us from baking a performance bottleneck into the new system before we'd even finished migrating.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were first splitting these three layers, was there a specific bug or incident that made it obvious the undifferentiated store was the problem, or did the architecture emerge more from anticipating pain before it happened?
cases.tonyRaw: It emerged from a real class of bugs rather than pure foresight — we had stale-state and re-render issues where updates from Liveblocks presence/cursors were getting tangled up with server-persisted data and local UI state all living in the same store, so a change in one would trigger invalidations or re-renders that had nothing to do with it. Once I traced a few of those back to the same root cause — the store not knowing the difference between "this is collaborative, ephemeral, and needs live sync," "this is server-truth and needs cache invalidation," and "this is just local UI state" — the three-layer split was the obvious fix rather than something I'd pre-designed. So it was reactive in origin, but once I saw the pattern I solo-owned restructuring it properly across all three layers rather than patching symptoms one at a time.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since Chrome extensions can't share cookies with your main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow — how were tokens issued, refreshed, and revoked across that boundary?
cases.tonyRaw: I solo-owned this piece, so I'll give you the actual flow. Since the extension runs on its own origin, cookies from the main app's session were a non-starter — I issued a bearer token at login that the extension stores and attaches as an Authorization header on every request into the backend API layer I built. Refresh was handled by checking token validity on incoming requests and issuing a new one before expiry rather than letting the extension silently fail mid-session, which mattered because a lot of the traffic through that layer was Liveblocks real-time sync and CRUD proxying for artifacts/meetings — you don't want a dropped token killing an active collaborative session. Revocation was server-side: invalidating the token on logout or account changes so the extension's next request gets rejected and forces re-auth. I'd want to double check the exact expiry window I set before quoting it precisely, but the core design was standard bearer-token-with-refresh, adapted specifically because the cookie-domain-sharing route was off the table.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing that state-management layer to feed AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model, what broke first when the AI generated content that didn't cleanly map to expected node types, and how did you handle malformed or unexpected structures at scale?
cases.tonyRaw: The first thing that broke was the assumption that AI output would respect our node schema at all — it would generate content with nesting or attributes that didn't correspond to any valid node type, and ProseMirror is strict about that, so naive insertion would throw or corrupt the doc. I co-led the team building this feature and personally designed the state-management layer, and the approach that held up was validating and normalizing AI output against the schema before it ever touched the document transaction, essentially treating it as untrusted input rather than assuming well-formed structure. We also had to account for two concurrent editor versions, so that normalization layer had to be version-aware rather than assuming a single fixed schema, which caught most of the edge cases before they became user-facing bugs.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Walk me through what actually broke when a long meeting transcript blew past the context window — was it truncation, degraded recall, or something more subtle — and how did your chunking strategy decide where to draw the boundaries?
cases.tonyRaw: What actually broke was degraded recall more than hard truncation — the model would technically still have tokens available, but relevant details from earlier in a long meeting would get crowded out or de-prioritized once we got deep into the transcript, so summaries and action items would skew toward whatever was most recent. I contributed to an existing agentic assistant rather than architecting it from scratch, and my specific piece was the transcript-chunking and context-window handling — I drew boundaries around natural conversational breaks rather than fixed token counts, so a chunk wouldn't split mid-topic and lose the surrounding context that made a statement meaningful. I also had to carry forward enough state between chunks — like who was speaking about what — so the model didn't treat each chunk as a cold start. It wasn't a perfect science; it was tuned against real meeting transcripts until recall held up consistently.

cases.interviewerQuestion: By what percentage did your chunking strategy improve reliability on long meetings?
cases.tonyRaw: I don't have a solid number I'd stand behind, so I won't make one up. What I can say concretely is what the change fixed: before, failures showed up as garbled output or dropped context on long meetings once the transcript hit the context window limit. Switching to try-full-transcript-first, only chunking on overflow, and splitting at sentence/speaker boundaries instead of a fixed character cutoff eliminated that class of failure in the cases I tested. If you need a hard reliability percentage, I'd want to go pull actual logs rather than guess.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the data model, what were the trickiest entity relationships to get right — and did any of those choices ripple into how you had to shape the GraphQL schema on top of it?
cases.tonyRaw: The trickiest part was modeling the relationship between a trader's identity and their trading performance data — a public profile needed to aggregate stats across accounts/time periods without leaking anything that should stay private to the trader's dashboard. I contributed to that data model design, and yeah, it definitely rippled into the schema: we ended up needing separate types for the public-facing aggregate views versus the underlying account-level data, rather than just exposing one model with field-level permissions. I helped build the GraphQL layer on top of that, but I want to be accurate — this was a team effort and not a feature I owned end to end, so I'd defer to teammates on some of the finer edge-case decisions in that model.
